War Without a Vote

As casualty counts were quietly revised and Congress split on ending the Iran conflict, tariffs, funding fights, and voting restrictions moved in parallel

```markdown This week began with a legal blow to gun-safety law and ended, five days later, with courts pushing back on multiple fronts against the executive branch — and in between came a war that grew larger in rhetoric while its official record grew smaller. Over seven days, the Iran conflict, immigration enforcement, tariff policy, and voting rights all advanced under executive pressure, while Congress, the courts, and the public tried, with mixed success, to hold the line.

The weekend set the tone. On Saturday, the Third Circuit became the first federal appeals court to strike down a state assault-weapons ban, breaking with every other circuit and teeing up a likely Supreme Court fight over similar laws in more than ten states. That same weekend, the Justice Department filed its first-ever application to a dormant 1996 tribunal allowing the Secretary of State to label noncitizens "alien terrorists" and deport them using evidence they never see — a revival of secret-evidence removal power with no operating history. Immigration enforcement turned deadly again when a federal agent with a documented history of domestic violence fatally shot a Colombian immigrant in Maine. Reporting soon showed that nearly half of more than 400 prosecutions against people accused of assaulting ICE agents had collapsed in court, and that the FBI had quietly stopped investigating fatal ICE confrontations altogether. Underneath it all ran a thread that would recur throughout the week: the Pentagon, it emerged, had concealed three earlier Iranian strikes on U.S. forces before a fatal attack in Jordan became public — an early sign that the war's true cost was being managed rather than reported. Amid it all, roughly 70 "ICE Out" rallies, nearly 700 voting-rights demonstrations, and more than 100 datacenter protests unfolded nationwide, and House Judiciary Chair James Comer acknowledged that the chamber was "basically done working" before the midterms.

Monday brought an unusually dense stack of developments. Trump signed proclamations imposing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian dairy, alcohol, and vehicles, actions Canadian officials called a violation of the USMCA trade agreement. He also reframed the Iran war's objectives after the World Cup final, saying the conflict had grown beyond its original scope, while separately vowing that Iran would "pay" for killed American soldiers — expanding war aims without new congressional authorization. That same event delivered a very different kind of headline: Trump was booed during the trophy ceremony, ushered off stage by FIFA's president, cropped from Spain's official victory photo, and denied handshakes by Argentine players — a public rebuke on a global stage. Domestically, ICE announced it would require body cameras for vehicle stops following fatal shootings in Texas and Maine, reversing an earlier push to cut camera funding by 75 percent. Investigative reporting revealed that SpaceX, Home Depot, Walmart, Toyota, and Google had donated hundreds of thousands of dollars to lawmakers sponsoring ICE-expansion bills, even as Citizens Bank cut credit lines to the two largest private detention operators, CoreCivic and The GEO Group. The administration also sought — then withdrew — subpoenas for New York Times reporters' phone records, including those of family members, tied to coverage of the Qatar-donated Air Force One. Gas prices crossed $4 a gallon for the first time since June, driven by the widening Iran conflict, while new executive orders tightened domestic-sourcing mandates for defense contractors.

By Tuesday, the war's financial and legal dimensions sharpened. Defense Secretary Hegseth testified before the Senate seeking a $454 billion increase to a $1.5 trillion total budget, even as senators caught him contradicting his own earlier claims that Iran's missile program had been "functionally destroyed." Joint Chiefs Chair Caine declined to rule out strikes on civilian infrastructure or further ground escalation. The same day, two separate court rulings tested executive removal power: a newly appointed U.S. Attorney sued after being fired less than an hour into the job, and a federal judge found the government had violated a fired civil servant's due-process rights, rejecting the claim that presidential removal authority overrides civil-service protections. Reporting also confirmed that ICE's year-old body-camera policy remained almost entirely unimplemented — only 3,000 of 13,000 officers were equipped despite adequate funding, a gap linked to at least eight enforcement deaths that went largely unrecorded. On a separate track, Trump declared Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu immune from arrest on U.S. soil after New York's mayor floated reviewing local authority under an ICC warrant. In Arizona, election deniers Alexander Kolodin and Andy Biggs won GOP primaries for the state's top election post and governorship, while Republicans nationally promoted federal voter-ID legislation using a widely mocked comparison to a restaurant's pasta-pass policy. Separately, reporting found the CDC had lost 25 to 30 percent of its staff, leaving the agency less prepared for disease outbreaks than before COVID.

Wednesday deepened both the war and voting-rights threads at once. House Republicans passed a budget resolution authorizing a $95 billion reconciliation package that combined Iran war funding, farm aid, and $10 billion toward the Save America Act — a bill that would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose strict voter-ID rules, using reconciliation specifically to bypass the Senate filibuster. The same day, Trump threatened to bomb a bridge or power plant in Tehran for every Iranian strike on shipping, and at a Dover Air Force Base ceremony for four fallen troops, he attributed views to the deceased while warning Iran would "pay a big price" — remarks widely seen as politicizing a solemn military ritual. Elsewhere, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's SNAP cuts stripped food assistance from 440,000 Arizonans, forcing mass caseworker layoffs and leaving vulnerable residents, including an elderly cancer survivor, without adequate food access. Des Moines and Tampa airports opted into a new program privatizing TSA screening, reviving a pre-9/11 model Congress had abandoned for safety reasons. House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan pushed the acting Attorney General to prosecute former special counsel Jack Smith, a move Smith's lawyers called retaliatory. The administration also approved a Saudi nuclear program and granted the UAE broad access to U.S. AI and semiconductor technology — decisions that would draw scrutiny within days.

Thursday was the week's most consequential day. The House passed a $1.15 trillion defense authorization bill embedding the same voting restrictions on a near party-line vote, then separately passed a concurrent resolution calling for an end to the Iran war, 214–208, joined by four Republicans — a symbolic assertion of war powers that carried no binding force absent Senate and presidential action. Trump told Israeli media and Axios he was close to ordering a strike "larger than any prior operation," saying Iran "haven't received enough pain yet," while Hegseth requested another $88 billion in supplemental funding, prompting a senator to ask whether the request functioned as a backdoor substitute for formal war authorization. That evening, the Pentagon's official casualty database dropped overnight from 18 deaths to 14; officials attributed the change to removing troops killed after a declared ceasefire, while a spokesperson cited "temporary data disruptions." Extensive reporting that day detailed a web of financial conflicts: a $2 billion Saudi investment in Jared Kushner's private equity fund coinciding with the new nuclear deal; UAE tech transfers approved over security objections tied to Kushner's holdings; a Pentagon AI office overseen by an official who had personally profited from crypto investments; a Pentagon private-equity arm tied to gains benefiting Trump's son; and outsized returns for Trump Jr. from a firm invested in government-linked companies. Compounding the strain, Brent crude jumped 42 percent in twenty days to above $100 a barrel following Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers, sending Treasury yields spiking and markets selling off. Twenty-five states and Washington, D.C. sued in Rhode Island over FEMA and DHS grant conditions tying more than $740 million in disaster and homeland-security funding to paper-ballot mandates, citizenship verification, and immigration cooperation. A separate suit challenged new tariffs on 60 countries as exceeding presidential trade authority. A federal panel allowed a Tennessee redistricting map splitting Memphis's majority-Black district — eliminating the state's only Democratic-held seat — to proceed under a weakened Voting Rights Act. ICE officers, including some Trump supporters, described denied leave, inadequate training, and chaotic leadership to reporters. And Vance Boelter was sentenced to two life terms plus 40 years for assassinating Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband.

Friday brought a wave of judicial pushback that stood in some contrast to the week's executive momentum. Federal courts halted the termination of work authorization for asylum seekers and TPS holders, dismissed an RNC lawsuit demanding sensitive New Jersey voter data, and paused the Paramount–Warner Bros. Discovery merger for 28 days pending antitrust review. The 25 attorneys general formalized their FEMA suit challenging the use of disaster aid as leverage over state election and immigration policy. The Fourth Circuit upheld the release of Georgetown scholar Badar Khan Suri, arrested by ICE over pro-Palestinian speech, affirming habeas rights in a ruling likely headed to the Supreme Court. Separately, the Electronic Privacy Information Center sued DHS over an unpublished policy tracking Americans who observed ICE operations, alleging retaliatory revocation of Trusted Traveler status. Trump threatened new tariffs against the EU over its fines against Apple, Meta, Amazon, and Google, opening a Section 301 investigation. Reporting revealed DHS had diverted $155 million of $170 million appropriated to counter Chinese illegal fishing toward World Cup and America250 security, without fully disclosing where the money went. Ahead of a rescheduled White House Correspondents' Dinner, 520 journalists signed a letter condemning threats to broadcaster licenses and the earlier subpoenas of reporters' families. Trump signed an order directing signage criticizing alleged bias in Smithsonian exhibits. Federal debt passed 100 percent of GDP, and the administration requested another $11.1 billion in farm aid. And in a final note of dissonance, Trump said he trusted Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping's personal assurances that they would not arm Iran — directly contradicting Hegseth's Senate testimony days earlier that both countries were enabling Iranian actions.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government stretching in several directions simultaneously: a war whose public accounting shrank even as its stated ambitions grew, a legislature that passed resolutions without the power to enforce them, and a string of policy vehicles — defense bills, disaster grants, budget reconciliation — used to carry voting restrictions that might not survive scrutiny on their own. Courts intervened repeatedly, but unevenly, blocking some assertions of executive power while allowing others, including a redistricting map that will shape political representation for years. Beneath the week's headline conflicts ran a quieter story of financial entanglement — family investments, foreign money, and defense-adjacent profit sitting close to decisions of state. None of it was hidden entirely; much of it was reported, argued over, and litigated in real time. Whether that scrutiny translates into accountability remains, as ever, a separate question from whether it occurred. ```
